subtopic_detail: Sequence of first-line manoeuvres when the anterior shoulder is impacted
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar attending a vaginal birth for a 35 year old para 2 who is being managed by the midwife. The last pregnancy had a birth weight of 4.1 kg with a difficult delivery. Second stage has lasted 90 minutes and the head is now born but retracts against the perineum. Restitution has not occurred. The midwife has already made a call for help and started the buzzer.

The next contraction is expected in about 40 seconds and you have declared shoulder dystocia to the team.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first manoeuvre?

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips onto the abdomen combined with a request to apply routine fundal pressure to expel the shoulder
options.rationale: McRoberts is correct but fundal pressure is absolutely contraindicated - it worsens shoulder impaction and increases the risk of uterine rupture and neonatal injury. Suprapubic pressure is the correct adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Zavanelli manoeuvre with cephalic replacement followed by emergency caesarean section as the first response to declared shoulder dystocia in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Zavanelli is a last-resort rescue after failed internal manoeuvres, associated with high foetal and maternal morbidity. It is never the first response. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Deliberate downwards traction on the foetal head with strong maternal pushing to attempt to disimpact the anterior shoulder immediately in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Increased downward traction on the head is the direct cause of brachial plexus (Erb's palsy) and clavicular injury in shoulder dystocia. Routine axial traction only is applied; force is never the answer. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Immediate deliberate fracture of the anterior clavicle to reduce shoulder diameter and permit delivery within the next contraction cycle in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Cleidotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre used only when all first- and second-line approaches have failed and there is no other route. Attempting fracture as first-line is inappropriate and unnecessarily traumatic. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips and suprapubic pressure directed downwards and laterally by an assistant while you attempt gentle axial traction with the next contraction
options.rationale: The Australian HELPERR/RANZCOG sequence starts with McRoberts (hyperflexion of hips to flatten the sacrum and rotate the pubic symphysis cephalad) plus suprapubic pressure directed downwards and laterally to dislodge the anterior shoulder from behind the pubis. Only routine axial traction is applied; excessive downward traction risks brachial plexus injury. If unsuccessful within 30 seconds, proceed to internal manoeuvres. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is declared when routine axial traction fails to deliver the shoulders after birth of the head. The RANZCOG HELPERR sequence is: Help (call), Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic - downward and lateral), Enter (internal rotational manoeuvres - Rubin II or Woods screw), Remove posterior arm, Roll (Gaskin all-fours). Each step is given 30 seconds before escalating. Force is not the answer - do not apply excessive traction, do not apply fundal pressure. Cleidotomy, symphysiotomy or Zavanelli manoeuvre are last resort. Team communication and clear time-stamped documentation are essential.
key_points: HELPERR: Help, Evaluate episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal), Remove posterior arm, Roll (Gaskin)
Never apply fundal pressure - worsens impaction
Only routine axial traction - excessive traction causes brachial plexus injury
30 seconds per manoeuvre before escalating
Time-stamped documentation and post-event debrief mandatory
explanation.pearls: The posterior arm delivery (Menticoglou manoeuvre) has the highest success rate of the internal manoeuvres and should be the primary internal step when first-line external manoeuvres fail in most contemporary AU teaching.

subtopic_detail: Combining latency antibiotics, corticosteroids and magnesium neuroprotection at extreme preterm gestation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 26 year old primigravida at 24 weeks and 3 days who presents with a gush of clear fluid and continued leaking. Speculum examination confirms pooling of amniotic fluid. She is afebrile and not contracting. She is very keen for everything possible to be done to give her baby a chance.

Her BMI is 22 and there is no history of urinary or genital infection during this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Speculum: pooling of clear amniotic fluid; cervix closed, long, no bleeding
data_table.CTG (variocam): baseline 145, variability appropriate for gestation, no contractions palpable
data_table.Ultrasound: single foetus 24+3, EFW 610 g, cephalic, AFI 4.2 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management bundle to commence in the next hour?

options.text: Immediate expedited birth by classical caesarean section at 24+3 given the extreme preterm gestation and risk of chorioamnionitis with expectant management in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Expectant management is offered at 24+3 without evidence of infection or foetal compromise, with continuous surveillance for chorioamnionitis and foetal wellbeing. Immediate delivery of a 610 g foetus has extremely poor outcomes without the benefit of corticosteroids or magnesium. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Latency co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg orally three times daily plus dexamethasone 12 mg IM stat and admission for observation only, without magnesium sulfate in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Co-amoxiclav is contraindicated in PPROM because of the necrotising enterocolitis signal from the ORACLE I trial - erythromycin is the correct AU choice. Magnesium neuroprotection is offered under 30 weeks per AU guidance and is a critical omission here. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Nifedipine 20 mg orally loading dose then 20 mg six-hourly for tocolysis and betamethasone alone; no antibiotics until symptomatic or biochemistry abnormal in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Tocolysis has no proven benefit in PPROM (it may prolong latency briefly but does not improve neonatal outcome) and can mask chorioamnionitis. Latency antibiotics improve neonatal outcomes and are not withheld until infection is manifest. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Latency erythromycin 250 mg orally four times daily for 10 days, betamethasone 11.4 mg IM stat (first dose), and IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour for neuroprotection while awaiting neonatology counselling
options.rationale: PPROM at 24+3 without infection warrants latency antibiotics (erythromycin - not co-amoxiclav which increases necrotising enterocolitis risk per ORACLE trial), antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart), and magnesium sulfate for foetal neuroprotection where delivery is anticipated within 24 hours before 30 weeks (Australian NNS/AAGBI recommendation extends to 30 weeks with MAGENTA data). Neonatology counsels the mother about survival and morbidity at extreme preterm gestation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Reassure and discharge home with weekly outpatient bloods and ultrasound; no admission or intervention required in the absence of infection or contractions in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: PPROM at extreme preterm gestation warrants inpatient admission for daily observation of temperature, uterine tenderness, CTG and inflammatory markers, and readiness to expedite birth for chorioamnionitis. Outpatient management is not standard AU practice. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

explanation.summary: PPROM before 24 weeks carries very poor prognosis - counsel about the futility threshold with neonatology involvement. Between 24 and 34 weeks, expectant inpatient management is standard, with latency antibiotics (erythromycin, 10 days), antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone), and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection where delivery is likely within 24 hours (under 30 weeks in Australian guidance). Continuous surveillance for chorioamnionitis (temperature, uterine tenderness, foetal tachycardia, rising inflammatory markers, purulent discharge) mandates expedited birth. Tocolysis is not standard. Beyond 34 weeks, expectant management for GBS-negative women is reasonable to 37 weeks; GBS-positive women deliver at 34-36 weeks.
key_points: Erythromycin (NOT co-amoxiclav - NEC risk) for 10 days latency
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 (24 hr apart) or dexamethasone 6 mg IM x 4 (12 hr apart)
Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection <30 weeks when delivery imminent
Inpatient surveillance for chorioamnionitis; deliver if infection develops
Tocolysis is not standard in PPROM
explanation.pearls: For PPROM approaching 34 weeks, the PPROMT trial supports expectant management to 37 weeks in GBS-negative women without infection, but jurisdictional practice varies; GBS-positive PPROM at 34 weeks typically triggers delivery with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.

subtopic_detail: Surgical management decision when the contralateral tube is already absent
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31 year old para 1 presenting with acute right iliac fossa pain and lightheadedness. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test is positive. She had a right ruptured tubal ectopic three years ago managed by right salpingectomy. This morning she completed her family planning with her partner, who was hoping for a second child but is prepared to accept whatever is safest for her.

On ultrasound the current pregnancy is in her only remaining tube.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 106/64, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Abdomen: peritonism localised to left iliac fossa, mild rebound
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus, 2.8 cm left adnexal mass with foetal cardiac activity present, moderate haemoperitoneum in pouch of Douglas
data_table.Prior surgical history: right salpingectomy 3 years ago for ruptured ectopic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative management?

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingotomy to preserve the only remaining fallopian tube, accepting the associated 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast risk
options.rationale: In a woman with a prior contralateral salpingectomy, the remaining tube is her only conduit for spontaneous conception, but the risk of recurrent ectopic in the SAME tube after salpingotomy is 15-20 percent, plus persistent trophoblast requiring further treatment. Contemporary RANZCOG and international consensus favour salpingectomy in this specific scenario because ART (IVF) bypasses the tube entirely and salpingotomy leaves a damaged residual tube that dominates recurrence risk. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Systemic methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM as the definitive treatment given the wish to preserve tubal function for future spontaneous pregnancy
options.rationale: Methotrexate is contraindicated - foetal cardiac activity is present, bhCG exceeds 5000 IU/L, there is significant haemoperitoneum and haemodynamic instability. Immediate operative management is mandatory. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy with counselling that IVF is the recommended route to future pregnancy, given that the residual tube carries a high recurrence risk
options.rationale: In a woman with prior contralateral salpingectomy, salpingectomy of the affected tube is preferred over salpingotomy because the recurrent-ectopic risk in the same (damaged) tube outweighs the loss of tubal fertility, and IVF bypasses the tubal factor entirely. This trickiness pattern (T14 historical bilaterality flip) inverts the standard 'preserve the tube' teaching. Counsel about IVF pathways preoperatively. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Emergency laparotomy with left oophorectomy in addition to salpingectomy to remove any ovarian source of the pregnancy in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Oophorectomy is not indicated in tubal ectopic pregnancy. Laparotomy versus laparoscopy is a decision based on stability and surgeon skill; laparoscopy is preferred if stable and appropriately equipped. Preserving the ovary is important for future ART cycles. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Ultrasound-guided direct methotrexate injection into the ectopic sac followed by monitoring, avoiding surgical trauma to the last remaining tube
options.rationale: Direct intralesional methotrexate is not standard practice and is contraindicated in unstable patients with active bleeding. Surgery is mandatory given haemoperitoneum, foetal cardiac activity, and haemodynamic compromise. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: The decision between salpingotomy and salpingectomy in tubal ectopic pregnancy hinges on the state of the contralateral tube. If the contralateral tube is healthy, salpingotomy preserves natural fertility potential and is preferred if surgeon-appropriate. If the contralateral tube is absent or diseased, contemporary evidence favours salpingectomy of the affected tube: the recurrent-ectopic risk in a damaged residual tube is high, persistent trophoblast complicates salpingotomy in 5-15 percent, and IVF bypasses tubal factors entirely with acceptable success. This inverts the intuitive 'preserve the tube' response. Preoperative counselling should explicitly discuss the IVF pathway.
key_points: Salpingotomy = preserved contralateral tube; salpingectomy = absent/damaged contralateral tube
Salpingotomy carries 5-15% persistent trophoblast + 15-20% recurrent ectopic in same tube
IVF bypasses tubal factor entirely - acceptable path to conception
Foetal cardiac activity, bhCG >5000, haemoperitoneum = surgery, not methotrexate
Counsel about IVF preoperatively when salpingectomy is planned
explanation.pearls: In tubal ectopic managed by salpingotomy, weekly bhCG monitoring to undetectable is mandatory - persistent trophoblast requires additional single-dose methotrexate or repeat surgery if bhCG plateaus above 5 IU/L.

subtopic_detail: Choosing between uterine artery embolisation and peripartum hysterectomy after failed conservative surgery
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in theatre with the consultant obstetrician, anaesthetist and haematologist for a 36 year old primipara who has bled 3.4 L after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. Uterotonics (oxytocin infusion, ergometrine 250 micrograms IM, carboprost 250 micrograms IM x3, and rectal misoprostol 800 micrograms) have failed. Bimanual compression and an intrauterine balloon achieved partial slowing. A uterine artery ligation with a B-Lynch brace suture has just been placed and bleeding continues at ~200 mL/5 min.

The interventional radiology suite is 15 minutes away and staffed within the hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 82/48 on noradrenaline 8 microgram/min, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 98% on 15 L NRB, temperature 35.8
data_table.Coagulation: fibrinogen 1.2 g/L (1.5-4.0), INR 1.6, platelets 78 x10^9/L, thromboelastography reduced maximum amplitude
data_table.Transfusion: 4 red cells, 4 FFP, 1 cryoprecipitate given; MHP activated 20 minutes ago
data_table.Airway: intubated after fifth unit red cells for ongoing haemorrhage
data_table.Family: primigravida, expressed wish for future pregnancy antenatally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscular every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses in total while awaiting the interventional radiology team
options.rationale: Carboprost has already been given at appropriate intervals with failure; escalating to further doses in a decompensating patient causes bronchospasm and hypertension without meaningful additional haemostatic effect. Definitive intervention is required. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Immediate intra-hospital transfer to interventional radiology for bilateral uterine artery embolisation as a fertility-preserving definitive intervention
options.rationale: Uterine artery embolisation is fertility-preserving and effective (85-95 percent success) but requires a haemodynamically stable patient who can tolerate the transfer and procedure. This patient is coagulopathic, hypothermic, requiring rising vasopressors, and bleeding ~200 mL every 5 minutes; transferring to the radiology suite risks decompensation in transit and delays definitive haemostasis. UAE is indicated for controlled ongoing bleeding in a stabilised patient, not for exsanguinating haemorrhage in theatre. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII (NovoSeven) 90 micrograms/kg as the next haemostatic intervention prior to surgical escalation
options.rationale: rFVIIa is an off-label rescue therapy considered only after correction of pH, temperature, calcium and fibrinogen and after all surgical options have been exhausted. It is expensive, prothrombotic (thromboembolic events 5-10 percent), and does not substitute for definitive surgical control. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Insert a second intrauterine balloon at higher inflation volume alongside the existing balloon to increase tamponade pressure
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is a single-device therapy; over-inflation risks uterine rupture and cervical injury. Sequential attempts at conservative measures that have already failed waste time in a decompensating patient. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Proceed immediately to peripartum hysterectomy given failure of all conservative measures and ongoing life-threatening haemorrhage
options.rationale: In refractory PPH with ongoing haemorrhage, escalating vasopressor need, coagulopathy and hypothermia, the priority is definitive haemostasis over fertility preservation. Peripartum hysterectomy is the appropriate life-saving step when the patient is already in theatre, intubated, coagulopathic and continuing to bleed. Transfer to interventional radiology in an unstable coagulopathic patient with continuing 200 mL every 5 minutes bleeding introduces unacceptable risk. The RANZCOG PPH stepwise pathway explicitly places hysterectomy as the final surgical option and time-to-decision is a mortality determinant. Fertility conversations occurred antenatally but survival dominates in decompensated shock. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG PPH management follows a stepwise algorithm: uterotonics, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, examination for genital tract trauma or retained products, bimanual compression and intrauterine balloon, uterine artery ligation and B-Lynch or similar compression suture, then uterine artery embolisation (if stable and transfer feasible) or peripartum hysterectomy. Each step is time-critical - PPH deaths cluster in the second hour of bleeding, and delay in progressing to definitive surgery is a modifiable mortality determinant. UAE is fertility-preserving but requires haemodynamic stability. Hysterectomy is the definitive intervention when the patient is exsanguinating, coagulopathic, and already in theatre - fertility conversations, however important, do not override the immediate need for survival.
key_points: PPH pathway: uterotonics → TXA → tamponade → suture → UAE/hysterectomy
UAE requires stability; hysterectomy for exsanguinating decompensation
Coagulopathy + hypothermia + rising vasopressor need = surgical control now
rFVIIa is last-resort adjunct AFTER surgical control
Time-to-definitive-haemostasis is a mortality determinant
explanation.pearls: Massive transfusion protocol activation aims for 1:1:1 red cells:FFP:platelets with fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate 3-4 g when fibrinogen <2 g/L), calcium replacement, and active warming; permissive hypotension is a trauma concept and does not apply to peripartum haemorrhage where uteroplacental perfusion needs pressure.

subtopic_detail: IV sodium bicarbonate threshold for QRS widening
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 25 year old woman brought in by her flatmate 90 minutes after finding empty amitriptyline packets and a suicide note. She had been prescribed amitriptyline 25 mg tablets for chronic migraine. She estimates 40 tablets ingested. She is drowsy but rousable and has vomited once en route.

Her flatmate confirms she has been increasingly withdrawn over recent weeks after relationship breakdown and university stress.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.ECG: sinus tachycardia rate 128, QRS 132 ms (upper limit 100 ms), terminal R wave in aVR 5 mm, no arrhythmia
data_table.Venous blood gas: pH 7.28, pCO2 34 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L (<2.0), potassium 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer 100 mmol (100 mL of 8.4 percent) IV sodium bicarbonate as a rapid push and repeat targeting QRS below 100 ms and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55
options.rationale: QRS widening beyond 100 ms in TCA overdose reflects sodium channel blockade and predicts VT/VF. The intervention is IV sodium bicarbonate boluses (1-2 mmol/kg, i.e. 100 mmol here) titrated to narrow QRS below 100 ms and to alkalinise pH to 7.45-7.55. Alkalinisation shifts drug away from cardiac sodium channels via protein binding and reduces free drug. This is a class I recommendation in the AU Toxicology & Toxinology Poisons Information text. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

options.text: Administer IV flumazenil 200 micrograms in 15 second increments to reverse sedation and reassess neurological status once alert
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures in a patient at risk of pro-convulsant drug effects; TCAs lower seizure threshold and flumazenil unmasks epileptogenic drug effects. It also does not reverse TCA toxicity. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

options.text: Give IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes to prevent progression to malignant ventricular arrhythmia in the context of QRS prolongation
options.rationale: Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics (procainamide, flecainide) and class III agents that prolong QT (amiodarone, sotalol) worsen TCA cardiotoxicity by further blocking sodium channels or prolonging repolarisation. Sodium bicarbonate is the specific antidote. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

options.text: Empirical activated charcoal 50 g orally now to reduce further absorption of the ingested tablets in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is considered within one hour of ingestion in patients with intact airway; at 90 minutes with reduced GCS the risk of aspiration outweighs the benefit unless the airway is secured. Sodium bicarbonate takes priority for the cardiotoxic manifestation. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

options.text: IV hypertonic 3 percent saline 100 mL over 30 minutes to correct the sodium status and stabilise cardiac membranes
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline does not have the same sodium-channel-shifting effect as bicarbonate because it does not alkalinise, and the therapeutic effect is combined sodium load AND alkalinisation. Bicarbonate is the specific treatment. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

explanation.summary: TCA toxicity produces anticholinergic, alpha-blocking, sodium channel blocking and CNS depressant effects. Cardiovascular toxicity is the leading cause of death: QRS widening beyond 100 ms predicts seizures, above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia. Management is airway (intubate if GCS deterioration), IV access, cardiac monitoring, IV sodium bicarbonate boluses (1-2 mmol/kg) titrated to QRS <100 ms and arterial pH 7.45-7.55, and correction of hypokalaemia (which worsens QT). Benzodiazepines for seizures. Lipid emulsion 20 percent 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus is considered in cardiac arrest or refractory shock. Avoid class Ia, Ic, and III antiarrhythmics; avoid flumazenil.
key_points: QRS >100 ms = give NaHCO3 1-2 mmol/kg IV, titrate to QRS <100 ms
Target pH 7.45-7.55 (alkalinisation dissociates drug from sodium channels)
Correct hypokalaemia (QT prolongation)
Avoid flumazenil, class Ia/Ic/III antiarrhythmics
Lipid emulsion for refractory cardiac arrest
explanation.pearls: The terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm and R/S ratio in aVR >0.7 predict severe TCA toxicity independently of QRS width and should trigger empirical alkalinisation even when QRS is <100 ms.

subtopic_detail: TGA pregnancy prevention program obligations before initiation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old woman with bipolar I disorder in your outpatient clinic. She is currently euthymic on lithium 750 mg nocte with a therapeutic level, but she describes intolerable weight gain and tremor. She and her consultant have discussed switching to sodium valproate. She is sexually active with a male partner and uses condoms inconsistently. She reports no current wish for pregnancy.

She asks whether she can start valproate today.

data_table.Contraception: condoms only, inconsistent use, no LARC
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): urea and electrolytes normal, TSH normal, lithium 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.0), pregnancy test negative today
data_table.Bipolar history: diagnosed age 20, one mixed episode, one manic episode, three depressive episodes; last episode 18 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily today given the current negative pregnancy test and plan to review in two weeks with an incremental dose escalation
options.rationale: Valproate carries a 10 percent congenital malformation risk and 30-40 percent neurodevelopmental disability risk in exposed pregnancies. The TGA and RANZCP guidance mandates that valproate is not initiated in a woman of reproductive potential unless highly effective contraception (LARC or dual method) is in place and a pregnancy prevention program is documented. A negative pregnancy test alone is not sufficient. (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention)

options.text: Commence sodium valproate at a low dose of 200 mg twice daily and prescribe oral folic acid 5 mg daily to mitigate neural tube defect risk in event of unplanned pregnancy
options.rationale: Folate supplementation does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity - valproate causes major malformations across multiple systems (neural tube, cardiac, craniofacial, limb) and neurodevelopmental disability by mechanisms beyond folate antagonism. Folate is used with all AEDs but is not a substitute for contraception. (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention)

options.text: Defer valproate initiation, refer for contraceptive counselling with a view to LARC (implant or intrauterine device) or documented dual method, complete a signed pregnancy prevention program acknowledgment
options.rationale: The TGA pregnancy prevention program for valproate requires that reproductive-age women initiating or continuing valproate have documented (a) counselling about teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks, (b) highly effective contraception in place, (c) annual specialist review, and (d) signed acknowledgment of understanding. LARC (etonogestrel implant or copper/hormonal IUD) is preferred. If she declines LARC, the recommendation is to use an alternative mood stabiliser (e.g. lamotrigine, atypical antipsychotic, remain on lithium with dose optimisation). (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention)

options.text: Add sodium valproate to her existing lithium as combination therapy to reduce individual dose exposure while allowing a broader mood stabiliser effect in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Combination therapy does not remove valproate's teratogenic risk and adds side effect burden. The valproate pregnancy prevention program applies regardless of dose or combination status. (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention)

options.text: Prescribe valproate but delay the first dose until she confirms she is menstruating this cycle to minimise the risk of exposure during a very early pregnancy
options.rationale: Menstruation does not confirm the absence of an ongoing pregnancy or prevent future pregnancy. The requirement is for documented ongoing highly effective contraception, not menstrual timing. (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is highly teratogenic (major malformations in 10 percent, neurodevelopmental disability in 30-40 percent of exposed pregnancies). Since 2019 the TGA has required a pregnancy prevention program for reproductive-age women, mirroring the UK MHRA Valproate PPP. Requirements are documented counselling about specific risks, highly effective contraception (LARC or dual method), annual specialist review, and signed acknowledgment. Prescribers should actively avoid valproate in reproductive-age women unless alternatives (lamotrigine, atypical antipsychotic, lithium) have been considered and rejected on clinical grounds. Folate supplementation does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity. Women already stable on valproate who become pregnant need urgent specialist review, not abrupt cessation which risks relapse.
key_points: 10% major malformations, 30-40% neurodevelopmental disability in exposed pregnancies
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandatory for reproductive-age women
LARC (implant or IUD) preferred; document counselling and acknowledgment
Folate does NOT mitigate valproate teratogenicity
Never abruptly cease in established pregnancy - urgent specialist review
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine is the preferred first-line mood stabiliser in reproductive-age women wishing to conceive because its bipolar depression prophylaxis is strongest and the malformation risk (~2 percent) is close to background; it needs 4-8 week uptitration to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
